Methods and Sources: Statistical Foundations of paweh

paweh package authors

Source: vignettes/paweh-08-methods-and-sources.Rmd
paweh-08-methods-and-sources.Rmd

How to use this reference

If your question is “How many people do I recruit?”, start with the study design below. If it is “Has anyone obtained this number independently?”, go to the published comparisons. A formula, an R function and a published numerical result are three different things. For example, the same function that reproduces a published requirement of 326 people can also calculate a design for which there is no published numerical benchmark.

Getting started introduces power (the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis under a specified alternative), the significance level (the intended rejection probability under the null), and minimum sample size (MSSN). The functions here plan studies. An expected genotype count, transmission count or test statistic in a design is not an observed association in patient data.

What is sampled and measured? Where to look
Unrelated cases and controls with called genotypes Case-control designs; recruitment is cases plus their controls.
An affected child and both parents, with called genotypes Transmission designs; the unit is a complete trio.
One or more continuous traits Quantitative traits; distinguish people screened from people selected for genotyping.
Sequence reads at specified depth Sequencing; cases and controls are called first, whereas the trio method uses read counts directly.
Genotype counts at one biallelic autosomal locus Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium tests observed counts or plans for a specified departure.
Routine measurements plus reference assessments for a subset LRTae; the four validation groups together make up the total enrollment.

A reading guide to the textbook

All numbered book sections and equations below refer to Gordon, Finch and Kim, Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics: How to Assess, Address, and Account for Mixtures in Association Studies (2020). The book connects the methods; the papers in the last column identify their origins or, where indicated, a related comparison. Follow the linked tutorials for inputs and executable examples.

Chapter and sections What to read for; package and primary sources
1. Introduction to Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics §§1.4.1–1.4.2: obtain genotype frequencies directly or derive them from risk. §§1.6.1.1–1.6.1.3 introduce the tests; §1.6.1.4 gives design noncentrality parameters (NCPs): Eq. 1.22 for the genotype test, 1.24 for trend, 1.25 for affected-child transmissions. See case-control (cc_power(): Pearson; Cochran; Armitage) and TDT (tdt_power(): Spielman et al.; Deng and Chen).
2. Overview of Genomic Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics §2.3 gives call-error models; §2.5.2 explains differential error (Gordon et al. 2002; Moskvina et al.). §2.7.1.2, Eq. 2.16 gives the case mixture in cc_mssn(). §§2.6.1–2.6.2 describe read probabilities relevant to sequencing; they do not supply the package’s case-control calling pipeline.
3. Phenotypic Heterogeneity §§3.3.1–3.3.2 explain how prevalence and diagnostic error change the genotype distribution among recorded cases. See Edwards et al. and case-control power.
4. Association Tests Allowing for Heterogeneity §§4.2.1.1–4.2.1.4 give the validation tiers, observed-data likelihood, statistic and example (Gordon et al. 2004; Barral et al.). Compare Ji et al. for prospective LRTae, including lrtae_ncp(). §§4.4.2.1–4.4.2.4 develop Kim’s trio read likelihood used for tdt_ngs_power(); §4.4.1 describes a different case-control read test.
5. Designing Genetic Linkage and Association Studies that Maintain Desired Statistical Power in the Presence of Mixtures For case-control planning, §§5.2.1–5.2.2 treat non-differential call and diagnosis errors; §5.3.1 treats locus mixtures. For trio planning, §5.2.5 treats genotype errors and null rejection, §5.2.6 phenotype errors (Buyske et al.), §5.3.3 unlinked families (Chen et al.). §5.4.4 covers Kim’s sequencing design. §5.2.3 studies LRTae power empirically; it is not the derivation of Ji’s analytical NCP.
6. Threshold-Selected Quantitative Trait Loci and Pleiotropy §§6.1.1–6.1.3 develop genotype means and tail probabilities (Falconer and Mackay); §6.1.4 covers ANOVA. §§6.2.1–6.2.2 develop the multiple-trait model, §6.2.3 joint thresholds and §6.2.4 the multivariate test. See the quantitative-trait tutorial and qtl_multivariate_mssn_full(). Gordon et al. (2017), rather than the book’s §6.2.4 example, supplies the 326-person comparison.

Unrelated cases and controls

The Pearson genotype test asks whether any of the three genotype proportions differ between groups (two degrees of freedom). The Cochran–Armitage trend test asks whether a specified genotype score differs on average (one degree of freedom). Scores of 0, 1 and 2 target an allele-dose trend; they can miss a strong heterozygote effect. cc_power() and cc_mssn() compare the expected groups at a specified control-to-case ratio. Both use large-sample approximations. The trend NCP scales the squared difference in mean scores by a pooled score variance; the sequencing design applies it to called genotypes.

Inputs. With model-based inputs, population allele frequency, Hardy–Weinberg proportions (the genotype proportions expected under random pairing of alleles), prevalence and genotype relative risks determine the two rows. With model-free inputs, supply the three genotype frequencies among true cases and among true controls in the same allele order. “Model-free” dispenses with an inheritance model; it still assumes the proposed rows represent the planned study and that people are sampled independently.

Change to the design What the comparison means
Genotype misclassification (Gordon et al. 2002; Ahn et al. 2007) Apply a transition matrix to each true genotype distribution. In the Douglas–Skol–Boehnke model (Gordon, Table 1b), a homozygote becomes heterozygous with probability γ; a heterozygote becomes either homozygote with total probability η. Set e1 = γ and e2 = η/2 (older notation: δ and ε/2). With γ = η = 0.10, the heterozygote row is 0.05, 0.90, 0.05. A direct switch between opposite homozygotes is excluded.
Differential genotype error (Moskvina et al. 2006) Different matrices for cases and controls can make identical biological distributions look different. Rejection at a nominal cutoff may then be a false positive. The package scenario illustrates this mechanism; it does not calibrate a new cutoff or reproduce a particular Moskvina simulation.
Phenotype misclassification (Edwards et al. 2005) A false negative moves a true case to the recorded controls; a false positive moves a true control to the recorded cases. Weight both contributions by population prevalence before conditioning on the recorded label. A 1% false-positive rate can seriously dilute the case group of a rare disease.
Locus heterogeneity (book §2.7.1.2) Only fraction pi of cases has the associated distribution; the remainder has the control distribution. Controls stay fixed. This shifts both genotype and trend contrasts. It assumes a control-like background for the other cases; it does not estimate membership.

The case-control tutorial shows these as separate sensitivity scenarios. For the narrower interfaces, each pair below computes fixed-sample power or solves for sample size:

Calculation Specialized exports
Genotype test, one error rate in every off-diagonal cell, including opposite homozygotes cc_chisq_power_genotype_misclassification_1p(), cc_chisq_mssn_genotype_misclassification_1p()
Two adjacent-call probabilities (Douglas–Skol–Boehnke) cc_chisq_power_genotype_misclassification_2p(), cc_chisq_mssn_genotype_misclassification_2p()
Three rates, allowing opposite homozygote calls cc_chisq_power_genotype_misclassification_3p(), cc_chisq_mssn_genotype_misclassification_3p()
Separate three-rate matrices by disease group cc_chisq_power_genotype_misclassification_differential_3p(), cc_chisq_mssn_genotype_misclassification_differential_3p()
Diagnosis error, supplied affected and unaffected genotype distributions cc_chisq_power_phenotype_misclassification(), cc_chisq_mssn_phenotype_misclassification()
Locus mixture, supplied associated and control distributions cc_chisq_power_locus_heterogeneity(), cc_chisq_mssn_locus_heterogeneity(); cc_trend_power_locus_heterogeneity(), cc_trend_mssn_locus_heterogeneity()

The first four pairs construct the underlying groups from a genetic model. Use the canonical interfaces for a genotype-error comparison with supplied group frequencies. Gordon and Edwards provide numerical checks below; the one- and three-rate sensitivity analyses are not additional replications.

Affected children and their parents

The transmission disequilibrium test (TDT; Spielman, McGinnis and Ewens) compares the two alleles that a heterozygous parent could transmit to an affected child. In prospective planning we need expected informative transmissions of the designated allele (ET) and expected informative non-transmissions (ENT). Neither counts all parents. For a planned set of independent trios, the affected-child NCP is (ET−ENT)2/(ET+ENT)(ET-ENT)^2/(ET+ENT) (Deng and Chen; book §1.6.1.4, Eq. 1.25). A larger NCP moves the test statistic farther from its null distribution.

Task in the TDT tutorial Interfaces and assumptions
Plan a clean or modified design tdt_power(), tdt_mssn(). Derive counts from frequency, risks, prevalence and marker–disease association, or scale externally supplied ET and ENT from a known number of trios. Counts alone cannot identify genotype-call errors.
Derive informative transmissions tdt_expected_transmission_probability(), tdt_expected_nontransmission_probability(), tdt_expected_transmission_counts(). Scale per-parent probabilities across the two parents. The helpers default to theta1 = pd; in the underlying equations theta1 is a recombination fraction. Set it to zero to match the canonical linked component. These defaults describe different designs.
Convert counts or a genetic model to a design tdt_power_from_expected_counts(), tdt_power_from_model(), tdt_mssn_from_model(). These expose the ordinary count/NCP steps; they are not new association tests.
Allow diagnostic false positives Buyske et al.; §5.2.6. Mix true affected-child families with families admitted by the screen. Prevalence determines the fraction of screen-positive children truly affected. tdt_mssn_phenotype_misclassification_from_ncp() starts with baseline NCP information. See the relative, not absolute, reproduction below.
Allow locus heterogeneity Chen et al.; §5.3.3. Mix linked families with an unlinked component with balanced expected transmission. Here heter_rate is the unlinked fraction. The comparison below uses 0% and 50%.

Genotype errors are a different calculation. In §5.2.5, especially §5.2.5.1, errors move calls by one allele copy. The model applies independent calls to all three family members, then conditions on calls consistent with Mendelian inheritance. Errors that pass that check can still bias transmission. The canonical model-based scenario extends the textbook’s null calculation to planning under association. In the tutorial illustration with 1% error per adjacent call, the required number rises from 215 to 249 retained trios and the null rejection rate at 600 trios is about 5.75% at nominal 5%. Neither number is an empirical error correction. Use one modifier at a time; these functions do not fit the observed-data TDTae or jointly model all three mechanisms.

Quantitative traits and pleiotropy

What if disease status is not observed because the outcome is continuous? A quantitative trait locus (QTL) shifts the distribution of a measurement. Pleiotropy means one locus can shift several traits. The quantitative-trait tutorial compares keeping each measurement with selecting only people in the extremes.

Design Exports and statistical basis
Model the trait qtl_falconer_parameters() derives genotype means and a common residual variance from the allele frequency, fraction of variance explained and dominance-to-additivity ratio. qtl_falconer_threshold_parameters() conditions genotype frequencies on eligibility for each tail. These are helpers for the Falconer model (Fisher; Falconer and Mackay; Lynch and Walsh; §§6.1.1–6.1.3).
Keep all observations qtl_anova_power(), qtl_anova_mssn(): a one-way ANOVA compares the three genotype means using a noncentral F distribution (Scheffé; §6.1.4). The calculation assumes independent observations, Hardy–Weinberg genotype frequencies and common within-genotype variance; sparse groups affect the approximation.
Genotype extreme individuals qtl_threshold_chisq_power(), qtl_threshold_chisq_mssn(): compare genotype frequencies in upper and lower tails using Pearson’s test. Reference-normal cutoffs are applied to a mixture of genotype-specific normals: the realized population eligibility need not be the nominal tail fraction. Li et al. provide related extreme-sampling context.
Measure several traits per person qtl_multivariate_power_full(), qtl_multivariate_mssn_full(): choose continuous Pillai MANOVA (Pillai; Gordon et al. 2017) or the joint-threshold genotype comparison (§§6.2.1–6.2.4). Supply a positive-definite within-genotype correlation matrix in trait order, not marginal correlations across all genotypes.

Pillai’s trace measures separation of the genotype-specific mean vectors relative to within-group variation; its design calculation uses the mean and covariance matrices. The threshold alternative selects people above every upper cutoff or below every lower cutoff. For each genotype, integrate its joint normal distribution over each corner, weight by genotype frequency, then compare genotypes between selected groups. Multiplying marginal tail probabilities is generally wrong for correlated traits.

paweh uses a univariate normal probability for one trait, deterministic Miwa–Hayter–Kuriki integration for 2–20 traits and randomized Genz–Bretz integration with a fixed local seed above 20. Inspect integration diagnostics, especially for small joint probabilities. These choices implement the probability calculation; neither the integration settings nor the tutorial’s joint-tail recruitment example is a published Pillai result.

Sequencing: genotype calls or raw reads?

The sequencing tutorial compares two data models. In both, depth is a fixed number of reads, not a mean over a distribution of depths. A per-read error is not the probability of calling the wrong genotype.

Case-control NGS. At depth vv and symmetric per-read error ee, the alternate-read count is binomial with success probability ee, 0.5 or 1−e1-e, given zero, one or two copies. ngs_genotype_error_matrix() assigns each possible count to its maximum-likelihood genotype, with a deterministic tie rule. Summing over counts gives a matrix with true genotypes in rows and called genotypes in columns. cc_ngs_power() and cc_ngs_mssn() transform each group’s genotype frequencies by its matrix, then compare mean called-genotype scores using the Ahn/Chapman–Nam trend NCP. The composition is specific to paweh. Ahn et al. start with given call-error probabilities; they did not propose this sequencing caller. Nor is this the raw-read LTTae,NGS in book §4.4.1.

Depth and base error may differ by case status. Diagnosis error or locus heterogeneity changes the distribution before sequencing; optional additional genotype error changes calls after sequencing. These are separate sensitivity scenarios. Even if the true groups are alike, different measurement processes can create a score contrast. More apparent power in that setting is not evidence for a biological effect.

Family TDT1-NGS. tdt_ngs_power() and tdt_ngs_mssn() retain uncertain reads. Kim (2015), Appendix B, weights the read likelihood over 15 ordered, Mendelian-consistent parental and child genotype configurations. The model uses independent trios, random mating and parental Hardy–Weinberg frequencies, conditionally binomial reads and multiplicative risk R2=R12R_2=R_1^2. The one-parameter NCP is N{log⁡(R1)}2IeffN\{\log(R_1)\}^2 I_{\mathrm{eff}}, with per-trio information evaluated under the null after allowing for nuisance parameters. Kim describes the benchmark effect as an odds ratio; paweh uses its numerical value as the one-copy risk in this model. The interface allows fixed depths by family role and directional base errors. A child with an ambiguous genotype still contributes through the possible family configurations.

The optional false-positive diagnosis and unlinked-family scenarios multiply Kim’s sequencing NCP by the ratio of modified to baseline ordinary TDT per-trio NCP coefficients (Buyske; Chen; §§5.2.6 and 5.3.3). These calculations use prevalence, maximal positive linkage disequilibrium (D′=1D'=1) and the bridge’s θ1=pd\theta_1=p_d setting. Each modifier is compared with the sequencing-only design. The ratio is a package approximation: it does not refit the raw-read likelihood or recalculate its information with misclassified children or unlinked families.

Validation subsamples and LRTae

Suppose everyone has routine disease and genotype measurements, but only a subset receives a more reliable assessment. LRTae is the likelihood ratio test allowing for error. Gordon et al. (2004) developed the double-sampling test; Barral et al. (2006) describe fitting it to observed data. Ji et al. (2005) is the source for prospective asymptotic power and sample size. The LRTae tutorial shows what can be planned without fitting a single observed patient record.

Function What it uses and returns
lrtae_ncp() Add expected information across four disjoint tiers: routine only, reference phenotype only, reference genotype only, both references. Remove the information shared with nuisance parameters (free case genotype frequencies and true control sampling share) by a Schur complement. The resulting quadratic form measures separation between the true case and control genotype distributions.
lrtae_power() Given tier counts, compare the corresponding noncentral chi-square distribution to the central cutoff (two degrees of freedom for three genotypes). The input concerns a proposed alternative, not an observed likelihood ratio.
lrtae_mssn() Given tier shares, find an integer total reaching target power. The Hamilton largest-remainder rule floors the four quotas and assigns remaining places in decreasing order of fractional remainder, breaking ties in tier order. This implements a specified allocation; it does not optimize the shares or cost.

Reference assessments are treated as truth. Routine error matrices are fixed planning inputs: a row conditions on a true state and sums to one over reported states. The genotype and phenotype errors combine independently given the true categories. If the information matrix is singular the design cannot identify the necessary contrasts. The package does not estimate error rates, fit the observed-data LRTae, or perform the distinct LTTae trend test (§4.2.2).

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium

The HWE tutorial introduces allele frequencies, genotype proportions, and their use in quality control. It derives the one-degree-of-freedom statistic by fitting one allele frequency after fixing the sample total. The null concerns genotype proportions in the sampled population. A departure can have several explanations, including ascertainment and errors in genotype calls.

Function Method and source
hwe_test() Uncorrected Pearson statistic with a fitted allele frequency, or a two-sided exact p-value obtained by conditioning on the allele count and summing tables at least as unlikely as observed. Wigginton et al. (2005) describe exact enumeration. Rohlfs and Weir (2008) give both statistics and the sparse-count example in Table 2.
hwe_power(), hwe_mssn() Pearson planning approximation with one degree of freedom and noncentrality NF2N F^2, from Rohlfs and Weir (2008). Fit the null at the observed alternative’s allele frequency. For call-error scenarios, obtain the observed alternative by postmultiplying true HWE proportions by a true-to-observed genotype matrix.

The textbook supplies background on HWE proportions (§6.2.2, p. 332), genotype-call errors (§2.3, pp. 57–58), and noncentral chi-square planning (§1.6, pp. 19–21). The notebook-based call-error example illustrates this package’s HWE planning model. Exact inference for observed counts and prospective Pearson power use different reference distributions.

Plots, dashboard and related software

The figures evaluate the underlying designs over a grid or display a model distribution. Their scientific sources are those of the corresponding rows above; a sensitivity curve is not another published statistical test.

Interface What is drawn
plot_cc_power(), plot_cc_mssn() Power or case recruitment as a case-control assumption changes.
plot_tdt_power(), plot_tdt_mssn(), plot_tdt_surface3d() Power or trio recruitment over one input or a two-input grid.
plot_tdt_power_phenotype_misclassification(), plot_tdt_mssn_phenotype_misclassification(); plot_tdt_power_locus_heterogeneity(), plot_tdt_mssn_locus_heterogeneity() Specialized views of the Buyske and Chen family sensitivities.
plot_qtl_genotype_distribution(), plot_qtl_anova_power(), plot_qtl_anova_mssn() Genotype-specific trait distributions and continuous-trait design curves.
plot_qtl_threshold_chisq_power(), plot_qtl_threshold_chisq_mssn() Power or recruitment among selected extremes.
plot_ngs_power(), plot_ngs_mssn() Sequencing sensitivity for the chosen case-control or trio design.
paweh_app() Opens the interactive dashboard. Read the unit and assumptions shown for the selected design; the app is an interface to calculations.

Other genetic study planners address related questions. USC’s Quanto includes gene–environment and gene–gene interactions. Michigan’s CaTS describes one- and two-stage association designs; its GAS Power Calculator adapts CaTS for one-stage studies. These are software references, not the source of the equations above or independent checks of the outputs below.

What has been reproduced?

The evidence attaches to a particular output at particular inputs. Exact published reproduction means agreement at the precision actually published; approximate published reproduction means close agreement with a stated difference. Relative-effect reproduction means that a ratio agrees while absolute results differ. A published-method implementation has a methodological source but no established match for the particular number. An illustrative calculation demonstrates a design without claiming a published numerical target. An unresolved comparison identifies what still needs independent evidence. Regression tests serve another purpose: they detect changes to a stored software result, even when its original source is uncertain.

Comparison and inputs Source, package result and evidence
Case-control genotype error — Gordon et al. (2002), Fig. 1b; equal groups, 95% power, nominal 5% Accurate calls: about 386 cases in the paper; continuous 386.0778, hence 387 whole cases in paweh (approximate). With γ = η = 10%: 477 cases in both (exact). Add an equal number of controls in each design.
Case-control phenotype error — Edwards et al. (2005); 250 per group, nominal 1%, no false negatives For (prevalence, false-positive rate) of (5%, 1%), (1%, 1%), (5%, 2%), (1%, 2%), the reported powers are 91%, 33%, 76%, 11%. paweh gives 91.35%, 33.20%, 76.34%, 10.98%: exact at published whole-percent precision.
Ordinary genotype error — Ahn et al. (2007), p. 257; 1,000 per group at nominal 0.001 Published trend/genotype powers about 0.88/0.81 (accurate calls) and 0.79/0.70 (5% adjacent transitions); calculated 0.8743/0.8061 and 0.7876/0.6992 (approximate). This checks the genotype-based calculation, not the upstream depth-to-call model.
Trio phenotype error — Buyske et al. (2009), p. 291; 1% prevalence, 0% versus 5% false positives Paper: 691 versus 27,118 trios. Package: 546 versus 21,401 whole trios. Recruitment rises about 39-fold in each (relative effect). The large absolute difference is unresolved; the corrected expressions in book §5.2.6 do not by themselves explain it.
Trio locus heterogeneity — Chen et al. (2009), Fig. 2; none versus half unlinked Paper: 3,430 versus 13,721 trios; package: 3,431 versus 13,723. Approximate (one and two trios higher). The cause has not been established; do not assume rounding explains it.
One quantitative trait — book §§6.1.3–6.1.4; allele frequency 0.15, QTL variance 0.025, dominance ratio 0.5 Exact recruitment targets: 996 for ANOVA on the tutorial’s grid (rounded genotype counts 720, 254, 22; package power 0.80005); 126 per tail, 252 genotyped in total, for the threshold test (power 0.80167). These matches do not validate every printed intermediate quantity.
Two continuous traits — Gordon et al. (2017), pp. 205–206; 80% power at nominal 5×10−85\times10^{-8} Exact: the paper reports 326 people. Package power crosses 0.80 between 325 (0.79847) and 326 (0.80149). The fractional root 325.5057 is a software value. At allele frequency 0.05 the expected two-copy group is only 326(0.05)2=0.815326(0.05)^2=0.815 people; a realized study may have none.
Two selected traits — tutorial’s joint upper/lower tails Illustrative: at 72 per group, power is 0.79606; at 73 it is 0.80563. This is a different design and parameter set from the 326-person reproduction.
TDT1-NGS — Kim (2015), Table 3 scenarios: allele frequency 0.35, per-read error 0.025, nominal 5×10−85\times10^{-8} At depths 4×/25×, all six stored values agree: 654/416 trios (90%, one-copy risk 2), 716/456 (70%, 1.8), 733/466 (10%, 1.5). Only the first pair is exact at the whole-trio precision reported in the published abstract. The other four match software benchmarks; comparison to the original table cells is unresolved.
LRTae — historical 500-person validation design Published-method implementation; illustrative numbers. Tier counts 248/135/72/45 yield NCP 22.40827 and power 0.99250. With the same shares, nominal 5% and target 80%, 216 people (107/58/31/20) give 0.80219. No complete workbook or matching published prospective output was independently verified.

Qualifications that matter for reuse

  • A matching recruitment target does not settle a parameter discrepancy. Book §6.1.3 prints 0.5 as a dominance deviation and −0.0985 as the zero-copy mean. Using 0.5 as the dominance-to-additivity ratio in §6.1.1 gives additive effect 0.227982, deviation 0.113991 and mean −0.097462. The univariate recruitment comparisons above still hold; the origin of the printed differences is unknown.
  • A similar observed example is not a prospective benchmark. Book §4.2.1.4, pp. 138–141, supports the LRTae genotype matrix, frequencies to printed precision and tier counts, but uses 5% of true cases recorded as controls rather than the tutorial’s 4%. Its statistic 24.1626 comes from fitting one dataset. Comparing it to the design NCP would answer the wrong question.
  • A test’s nominal level is conditional on the measurement model. Differential call errors can produce a case-control contrast under the biological null. Mendelian consistency does not remove all erroneous trio calls. Rare genotypes, selected tails and rare informative transmissions may also undermine large-sample approximations. Check the expected counts and interpretation of rejection before using a recruitment target.
  • Keep the denominator and units with every result. Prevalence refers to the population, not the fraction of cases recruited. For extreme sampling, a quota of genotyped people is not the number screened. A trio count is neither a participant count nor an informative-parent count. None of the design calculations propagates arbitrary uncertainty in pilot inputs; vary plausible input values before committing to a study size.
